summary: Updates RFC 4944 with a paging mechanism for 6LoWPAN header compression, which carries IPv6 over small low-power wireless networks. A new Paging Dispatch switches between sets of compression codes, making room for future extensions.

eli5.summary: Small wireless sensors send tiny messages and have few shorthand codes. This adds page numbers, like flipping to a new page in a code book, so more shorthand fits.

subtitle: A page-number switch that gives 6LoWPAN header compression room to grow without breaking old devices.

tldr.problem: The dispatch byte that tells a 6LoWPAN parser what kind of header comes next was running out of values as more protocols needed to be compressed.
tldr.mechanism: A new Paging Dispatch with bit pattern 11 11xxxx selects one of 16 Pages, each a separate parsing context for dispatch values. Page 0 is the default, so existing packets still parse the same way.
tldr.outcome: Pages 1 to 14 are open for future allocations, Page 15 is reserved for Experimental Use, and Page 1 already carries the LOWPAN_IPHC values. The RFC updates RFC 4944.

today: RFC 8025 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why 6LoWPAN Needs Paging
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are designed first of all to save energy, because devices often run on primary batteries that must last for years or on very small amounts of scavenged energy. Sending less data is one way to save energy.

Frames in many LLN standards are far smaller than the IPv6 maximum transmission unit of 1280 bytes. A network using the classical physical layer of IEEE 802.15.4 is limited to 127 bytes per frame, which is why compressing IPv6 packets led to the 6LoWPAN Header Compression work in RFC 6282.

As more protocols need compression, the encoding capacity of the original dispatch defined in RFC 4944 and RFC 6282 becomes saturated. This RFC adds a context switch mechanism, expressed as Pages and signaled by a new Paging Dispatch.
sections.eli5: A small gadget can only send a few bytes at a time, so it uses short codes. The list of short codes was nearly full, so this RFC finds a way to make more.

sections.title: Pages as Parsing Contexts
sections.content:
The RFC adds the idea of a parsing context to the 6LoWPAN parser, where each context is identified by a Page Number. It defines 16 Pages.

Pages are delimited inside a packet by a Paging Dispatch value that names the next current Page. A Page N becomes active once its Paging Dispatch is parsed, and it stays active until another Paging Dispatch is parsed.

The dispatch values defined in RFC 4944 belong to Page 0. Page 0 is the default and does not need to be signaled at the start of a packet, which keeps existing implementations working. Those same Dispatch bits are free to be reused in Pages 1 to 15.
sections.eli5: Think of a code book with 16 pages. Every message starts on page 0, so old readers know what to do. A special note can say turn to page 1, and from then on the same short codes mean new things.

sections.title: The Paging Dispatch Byte
sections.content:
A Paging Dispatch is one byte with the bit pattern 11 11xxxx, where xxxx is the Page Number from 0 to 15. That uses the values 11 110000 through 11 111111.

The RFC does not use the Escape Dispatch, which would extend Page 0 to more values. A single packet can hold several occurrences of a new header indexed by this specification, and spending an extra octet on an Escape Dispatch each time would be prohibitive. The Paging Dispatch is instead present in all Pages, including Page 0 and Pages defined later.
sections.eli5: The page note is one byte. The first four bits say this is a page note, and the last four bits give the page number, from 0 to 15.

sections.title: Page 1 and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Page 1 has special properties. The dispatch bits defined for LOWPAN_IPHC in RFC 6282 have the same values in Page 1, so a packet encoded per RFC 6282 can be decoded without switching from Page 1 back to Page 0.

Mesh Headers carry Layer 2 information and are processed before Layer 3 information encoded in Page 1. If a packet needs a Mesh Header, it MUST be placed before the first Page 1 Paging Dispatch, if any. Fragment Headers from RFC 4944 have the same requirement.

The NALP dispatch pattern is only defined for the first octet of a packet, so switching back to Page 0 for NALP inside a packet makes no sense. As a result, the Page 0 Paging Dispatch 11 110000 may not actually occur in packets that follow the 6LoWPAN specifications available when the RFC was written.
sections.eli5: Page 1 keeps the old shorthand codes, so nothing needs to change for packets that already work. Some older notes, like routing and chopping-up labels, must come before the page-turn.

sections.title: Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA allocates 16 values for Page switch from the Dispatch Type Field registry created by RFC 4944, from 11 110000 through 11 111111, representing Page Numbers 0 through 15.

The registry also gets a new column called Page. Existing content is assigned to Page 0. The LOWPAN_IPHC values, 01 100000 through 01 111111, have the same definition in Page 1 as in Page 0, so Pages 0 and 1 are grouped together for that range.

Values in Page 15 from 00 000000 to 11 101111, which is everything except the Page switch space, are reserved for Experimental Use and shall not be assigned. Pages 1 to 14 are to be assigned for new protocols. Future assignments follow the Specification Required policy, which is expected to make it easier for non-IETF organizations to obtain assignments.
sections.eli5: The official list of codes gets a new column for the page number. Old codes go on page 0, page 15 is kept for experiments, and the pages in between are saved for later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds nothing of its own here. It says only that the security considerations of RFC 4944 and RFC 6282 apply.
sections.eli5: This change adds no new safety rules. The safety rules from the earlier documents still apply.
